 1                      SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT (STANDING ORDER I.C)

 2   I.       THE COURT LACKS PERSONAL JURISDICTION OVER DEFENDANTS

 3            This action is a blatant attempt by Plaintiffs’ counsel to evade a May 2, 2024 decision by

 4   Judge Sunshine S. Sykes of the United States District Court for the Central District of California,

 5   which dismissed, with prejudice, identical claims against Defendants for lack of personal

 6   jurisdiction in California. Muto v. Fenix Int’l Ltd., No. 5:22-cv-02164-SSS-KK, 2024 WL 2148734

 7   (C.D. Cal. May 2, 2024) (“Muto”). Rather than move for reconsideration or appeal that dismissal,

 8   Plaintiffs’ counsel refiled a carbon copy of the Muto Complaint that Judge Sykes ordered dismissed

 9   under the guise of two new Plaintiffs, one of whom is a resident in the Central District of California.
10   This Court should not entertain such transparent attempts to forum shop.1 Instead, the Court should

11   dismiss Plaintiffs’ claims for lack of personal jurisdiction for the same reason that Judge Sykes

12   dismissed Plaintiffs’ previous attempt to bring these claims against Defendants: Plaintiffs’

13   assertions that a significant number of California residents visited and purchased subscriptions

14
     1
15     Typically, the vehicle to dissuade this type of behavior is a motion to transfer venue pursuant to
     28 U.S.C. § 1404(a). Courts in California routinely grant motions to transfer when presented with
16   this type of blatant forum shopping. See e.g., Forrand v. Fed. Express Corp., 2008 WL 276389, at
     *3 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 31, 2008) (“This Court cannot reach the incredible conclusion that counsel
17   representing a plaintiff who resides in the Central District, where counsel had previously filed a
18   lawsuit asserting claims on behalf of a putative class that included the plaintiff, were not engaged
     in forum shopping when they chose to file a nearly identical class action in the Northern District
19   days after the judge in the earlier-filed Central District case issued an unfavorable ruling.”); Meza
     v. Procter & Gamble Co., 2023 WL 3267861, at *4 (C.D. Cal. Apr. 27, 2023) (“there is an equally
20   strong inference of forum shopping when the parallel actions are filed by the same law firm, and
     such strategic machinations by plaintiff’s counsel are equally discouraged”); Trottier v. FieldCore
21   Servs. Sols., LLC, 2020 WL 13304063, at *5 (C.D. Cal. Aug. 3, 2020) (finding inference of forum
22   shopping when plaintiff's counsel filed the action “with a new plaintiff” after receiving an
     unfavorable ruling in another district); LegalForce, Inc. v. Legalzoom.com, Inc., 2018 WL 6179319,
23   at *3 (C.D. Cal. Nov. 27, 2018) (“Forum shopping could reasonably be inferred if the plaintiff files
     the same or similar case represented by the same law firm in a different district after receiving
24   unfavorable rulings there.”); Williams v. WinCo Foods, LLC, 2013 WL 211246, at *7-8 (E.D. Cal.
     Jan. 10, 2013) (finding that filing of similar lawsuits involving the same claims on behalf of “nearly
25   an identical class” by the same counsel suggested forum shopping and discussing cases holding
26   similarly). However, a threshold requirement of transferring a case pursuant to Section 1404(a) is
     that the Defendant is subject to personal jurisdiction in the transferee court. Given that, as Judge
27   Sykes correctly ruled in Muto, Defendants are not subject to personal jurisdiction anywhere in
     California for Plaintiffs’ claims, a motion to transfer under Section 1404(a) is not available to
28   Defendants.

 4   II.     OTHER GROUNDS FOR DISMISSAL

 5           In addition, there are other independent grounds for dismissal— forum non conveniens, lack

 6   of standing, and failure to state a claim as to Fenix Internet—that Defendants raised in its previous

 7   motion to dismiss the original action in the Central District. Defendants maintain that Judge Sykes’s

 8   personal jurisdiction analysis should end this Court’s inquiry. Should this Court find it necessary to

10               Plaintiffs Must Bring this Suit in the United Kingdom: The forum-selection clause in

11   the OnlyFans Terms of Service—to which each of the Plaintiffs agreed when they created their

12   OnlyFans accounts—requires Plaintiffs to bring this suit in the United Kingdom (where OnlyFans

13   is operated) and mandates dismissal of this action pursuant to the doctrine of forum non conveniens.

14               Plaintiffs Lack Standing to Bring their Claims: Plaintiffs’ conduct demonstrated their

15   understanding that their OnlyFans subscriptions renewed. Each named Plaintiff regularly

16   subscribed to and subsequently canceled dozens of OnlyFans subscriptions before their renewal

17   date (often, almost right away). In some instances, they later re-subscribed to the same content and

18   again canceled before the renewal date. None of FIL’s or Fenix Internet’s alleged violations caused

19   Plaintiffs’ injury. Thus, Plaintiffs cannot establish either constitutional or statutory standing.
20               Plaintiffs Fail to State a Cause of Action Against Fenix Internet: Plaintiffs plead no

21   facts showing that Fenix Internet violated any statute the Complaint attempts to assert.

 8           A.      FIL, Fenix Internet, and OnlyFans

 9           FIL is a company incorporated and registered in England and Wales, with its headquarters
10   in London. Decl. of Lee Taylor in Support of Fenix Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss (“Taylor Decl.”)

11   ¶ 3. FIL owns and operates OnlyFans, a leading content-sharing and social media website that

12   allows users (i.e., “Fans”) from around the world to subscribe to and engage with content (such as

13   videos, music, and photographs) produced by content creators (“Creators”) who are also located

14   around the world. Id. ¶¶ 3, 13.

15           Fenix Internet is a separate company organized under the laws of Delaware, with its

16   registered office in Delaware. Id. ¶ 4. Fenix Internet does not operate OnlyFans; instead, it holds

17   banking and payment processing relationships on behalf of its parent company, FIL. Id. ¶¶ 5-6.

18   Specifically, at FIL’s direction, Fenix Internet collects payments from third-party processors and

19   distributes the money it collects (through other third-party providers) to Creators. Id. ¶ 6. Neither
20   FIL nor Fenix Internet is registered to do business in California. Id. ¶ 10. Neither has any offices or

21   employees in California. Id. ¶ 7. Neither engages in marketing, sales, or commercial activity

22   targeted specifically at California residents. Id. ¶ 8.

26   stating: “By signing up you agree to our Terms of Service ...” ECF 1 ¶ 29. That same disclosure

 1   III.    ARGUMENT
 2           A.     Plaintiffs’ Complaint Should be Dismissed for Lack of Personal Jurisdiction.

 3           For the same reasons set forth in Judge Sykes’s May 2 Order, this Court should dismiss

 9           16.        The ARL seeks to ensure that, before there can be a legally-binding automatic
10   renewal or continuous service arrangement, there must first be clear and conspicuous disclosure
11   of certain terms and conditions and affirmative consent by the consumer. To that end, § 17602(a)
12   makes it unlawful for any business making an automatic renewal offer or a continuous service
13   offer to a consumer in California to do any of the following:
14                      a. Fail to present the automatic renewal offer terms in a clear and conspicuous
15   manner before the subscription or purchasing agreement is fulfilled and in visual proximity to the
16   request for consent to the offer. For this purpose, “clear and conspicuous” means “in larger type
17   than the surrounding text, or in contrasting type, font, or color to the surrounding text of the same
18   size, or set off from the surrounding text of the same size by symbols or other marks, in a manner
19   that clearly calls attention to the language.” The statute defines “automatic renewal offer terms”
20   to mean the “clear and conspicuous” disclosure of the following: (1) that the subscription or
21   purchasing agreement will continue until the consumer cancels; (2) the description of the
22   cancellation policy that applies to the offer; (3) the recurring charges that will be charged to the
23   consumer’s credit or debit card as part of the automatic renewal plan or arrangement, (4) the
24   length of the automatic renewal term or that the service is continuous; and (5) the minimum
25   purchase obligation, if any.
26                      b. Charge the consumer’s credit or debit card for an automatic renewal or
27   continuous service without first obtaining the consumer’s affirmative consent to the agreement
28   containing the automatic renewal offer terms, including the terms of an automatic renewal offer
